tool.name: Node.js
tool.tagline: JavaScript runtime for servers, command-line tools and build tooling
tool.description: Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser, on your own computer or a server, and adds built-in tools for files, networks and starting other programs. It powers web servers, command-line tools and build systems, and its package manager, npm, offers millions of ready-made packages. Learning Node lets you use one language across the whole web stack.

glossary.def: A module that ships inside Node.js itself, such as node:fs for files, so you can import it without installing anything.
Long-Term Support: a Node.js version that gets bug and security fixes for about three years. Every even-numbered version (20, 22, 24) becomes one.
JavaScript with added notes saying what type each value should be. A checker reads those notes to catch mistakes before the code runs.
A first line like #!/usr/bin/env node in a script file, telling macOS or Linux which program should run the file.
A JavaScript file that shares code with the standard import and export keywords: the modern module system used by browsers and Node.
The package manager that comes with Node.js. It downloads packages from the public npm registry into your project and runs your project's scripts.
The file at the top of a Node project that names it and lists its settings, its scripts and the packages it needs.
The folder where npm puts the packages a project installs. It is recreated by npm install, so you never edit it or save it with your code.
A command that comes with npm and runs a package's command-line tool, using the copy installed in your project if there is one.
npm's lock file: it records the exact version of every package installed in a project, so every later install gets the same set.
Node's type for a fixed-length chunk of raw bytes, used for file contents, network data and anything that isn't text.
A short notice the operating system delivers to a running program, such as 'please stop' when you press Ctrl+C. The program can react to it or be stopped.
The 'interrupt' signal a program receives when you press Ctrl+C in its terminal; by default the program stops.
A built-in object for cancelling work: give its signal to an operation such as fetch, then call abort() and that operation stops and rejects.
Node's class for objects that announce named events; other code registers listener functions that run each time an event is emitted.
A stream setting in which each chunk can be any JavaScript value, such as an object, instead of bytes or text.
The HTTP client library built into Node; it powers the global fetch function.
Node's built-in debugging service. A debugger such as Chrome DevTools or VS Code connects to it to pause and examine your running program.
The developer tools built into the Chrome browser. Besides web pages, they can attach to a Node program to debug it and measure its speed and memory.
A debugger marker on a line of code that prints a message each time the line runs, without pausing the program.
A completely separate copy of the V8 JavaScript engine with its own memory. Each worker thread runs in its own isolate.
The C library inside Node.js that talks to the operating system for files, network and timers, and runs Node's event loop and its small pool of helper threads.
A small job, such as the code after an await or a promise's then callback, that runs as soon as the current code finishes, before timers or I/O callbacks.
A stream's buffer threshold: once this much data is waiting, the stream signals the side producing data to pause.
Node's built-in module that starts several copies of your program as separate processes and spreads incoming connections between them, so a server can use every processor core.
A separate program started by your program, which is called its parent. The parent can send it input, read its output and stop it.
Inter-process communication: a channel two running programs use to send messages to each other.
A chart of a CPU profile where each bar is a function and its width shows how much time was spent in it, so the widest bars show where the time goes.
How late callbacks run compared with when they were due. A high value means something is keeping Node's single JavaScript thread busy.
Node's opt-in lockdown mode (--permission): the program can't read or write files, start other programs or start threads unless you allow it.
An attack where a file name such as ../../etc/passwd climbs out of the folder you meant to serve and reaches other files.
An attack where untrusted input sets properties on the object every other object inherits from, silently changing how the whole program behaves.
Regular-expression denial of service: text crafted so a badly written regular expression takes an enormous time to check, freezing the program.
An attack that makes a service unusable for everyone, for example by flooding it with requests or sending input that takes forever to process.
All the packages and tools your project depends on, and the people who publish them. A supply-chain attack slips harmful code into one of them.
A saved record of every object in a program's memory at one moment and what refers to what, used to hunt memory leaks.
The part of V8's memory where new objects are created. It is cleaned often and cheaply, because most objects are short-lived.
The part of V8's memory for objects that have survived a few clean-ups. Its maximum size is set with --max-old-space-size.
Resident set size: all the memory the operating system has actually given a process, including memory outside the JavaScript heap.
In a heap snapshot, an object that holds a reference to another one and so keeps it from being freed by the garbage collector.
A ready-built C, C++ or Rust library packaged as a .node file that Node loads like a module, letting JavaScript call that code.
Node's stable C interface for writing native addons. An addon built against it keeps working on later Node versions without being rebuilt.
Application binary interface: the low-level rules by which ready-built program files call each other. While those rules stay the same, old files keep working without being rebuilt.
In a native addon, a short-lived region in which the JavaScript values your C++ code holds stay valid; they are released when it ends.
A compact format for ready-built code that browsers and Node can run safely at close to native speed. It is often built from C, C++ or Rust.
A Node class that keeps a value, such as a request ID, attached to one chain of asynchronous work, so any function in that chain can read it without being passed it.
Node's low-level module for watching every asynchronous operation as it is created and run; AsyncLocalStorage lives in it and is built on it.
To replace a function inside someone else's code from the outside while the program runs, in order to change or observe what it does.
Application performance monitoring: tools that measure a live service's speed and errors request by request and show them on dashboards.
Keeping a network connection open after a response, so the next request to the same server can reuse it instead of connecting again.
The first process started in a container or on a machine. It has special duties, such as passing stop requests on to other programs.
The program that starts, supervises and restarts background services on most Linux systems.
A system that runs containers across many machines, restarts them when they fail, and starts or stops copies to match the load.
An expected failure in a correct program, such as a missing file, a refused connection or bad user input, that the code should handle.
A bug in the code itself, such as calling something that isn't a function. The program can't sensibly recover; log it and restart.

concepts.name: What Node.js is
concepts.summary: Node.js lets JavaScript run on your own computer or a server, not just in a web page, and adds built-in tools for files and networks.
concepts.why: Knowing what Node adds to JavaScript, and what it leaves out, tells you which code will work in it and why it handles waiting the way it does.
concepts.body:
In a browser, JavaScript works with a web page but is deliberately kept away from the rest of the computer: it can't read your files or start other programs. **Node.js** is a program that runs JavaScript anywhere else — on your laptop or on a server — and adds those missing abilities. Software that runs code for you like this is called a **runtime**.

Inside, Node uses **V8**, Chrome's JavaScript engine, so the language is the JavaScript you know. Around it, Node adds **built-in modules**: modules that ship with Node itself, such as `node:fs` for files and `node:http` for answering web requests. You import them like any other module, with nothing to install.

What changes is the environment:

- There is no `window`, no `document`, no DOM — there is no page to show.
- Many browser features exist anyway: `fetch`, `URL`, `setTimeout`, `console`.
- Your program runs as a **process**: one running copy of a program, which the **operating system** (Windows, macOS or Linux — the software that runs the computer) starts and stops.

Node's big idea is about waiting. Reading a file or waiting for a reply over the network is slow compared with running code. This kind of reading and writing is called **I/O** (input/output). When your code asks for I/O, Node hands the job to the operating system and carries on running other JavaScript instead of standing idle. That is **non-blocking** I/O.

When the result is ready, Node runs your callback or resumes your `await`. The part of Node that keeps track of what is waiting and runs whatever is ready next is the **event loop**. Like one waiter serving many tables, one Node process can look after thousands of slow network connections at once — which is why Node is popular for servers and developer tools.

The flip side: your JavaScript itself runs one step at a time. A long calculation, say crunching a million numbers in a loop, keeps Node busy, and nothing else happens until it ends. Node is great at waiting, less so at heavy number crunching (a later lesson shows how to move that work elsewhere).

This course targets **Node.js 22 LTS**. LTS (Long-Term Support) versions get bug and security fixes for about three years. Use an LTS version for anything real; check yours with `node --version`.
takeaways: Node runs JavaScript outside the browser: same language, no DOM, plus built-in modules
Your program is a process that the operating system starts and stops
I/O is non-blocking: Node does other work while it waits
Long calculations hold everything up; run an even-numbered LTS release
pitfalls: Expecting browser objects like `window` or `document` to exist.

quiz.q: Why can a single Node process serve thousands of slow web visitors at once?
options: It starts a separate copy of itself for every visitor
V8 runs every visitor's code at the same instant
While it waits on I/O it keeps running other code, then handles each result when it is ready
It makes visitors wait in line and serves them one at a time
quiz.explain: Node hands the waiting to the operating system and keeps working, so an idle connection costs almost nothing.

concepts.name: Running scripts, the REPL and --watch
concepts.summary: Run files with node, experiment in the REPL, try one-liners, and restart automatically when you save with --watch.
concepts.why: These are the commands you use every day while writing and fixing Node code.
concepts.body:
The simplest way to run code is `node app.js`. A file of code you run directly like this is called a **script**. Node runs it top to bottom, then keeps the process alive as long as there is still work pending — an open server, a timer, an unfinished file read. When nothing is left, the process ends on its own.

Running `node` with no arguments opens the **REPL** (read–eval–print loop) you met in JavaScript. It is ideal for trying out a function quickly:

- `_` holds the last result; `.help` lists commands; `.editor` lets you paste several lines; `.exit` or Ctrl+D quits.
- Top-level `await` works, and built-in modules are already loaded: type `fs.` and press Tab.

For quick one-offs use `-e` (evaluate) or `-p` (evaluate and print the result):

```bash
node -p "os.cpus().length"
node -e "console.log(process.versions.v8)"
```

While developing, `node --watch app.js` restarts the program whenever the file, or anything it imports, changes — no add-on tool needed. Add `--watch-path=./src` to watch a whole **directory** (another word for folder).

Useful companions:

- `node --run dev` runs a command named `dev` listed in your project's `package.json` settings file (you'll meet it soon).
- `node --check file.js` only reads the file without running it, catching **syntax errors**: grammar mistakes, like a missing bracket, that stop code from running at all.
- `node --env-file=.env app.js` loads settings from a file (covered later).

Since version 22.18, Node can also run **TypeScript** files directly (`node app.ts`). TypeScript is JavaScript plus notes saying what type each value should be; Node simply deletes those notes and runs the rest. It never checks them, so keep TypeScript's own checker, `tsc`, for that.

On macOS and Linux, a script can start with the line `#!/usr/bin/env node` (a **shebang**), which tells the system to run the file with Node. Mark the file as runnable with `chmod +x greet.js` and you can start it with `./greet.js`, like any other command.
takeaways: `node file.js` runs a script; the process ends when no work is pending
The REPL supports top-level await and has built-in modules preloaded
`--watch` restarts on changes; `--run` runs commands listed in package.json
pitfalls: Thinking `--watch` or running TypeScript directly checks your types — they only restart the program and strip the type notes.

quiz.q: A script calls setInterval and nothing else. What happens when it reaches the last line?
options: The process stays alive because the interval is pending work
Node throws because the event loop is still busy
The interval runs once and the process ends
quiz.explain: Active timers (and open servers or connections) give the event loop work to do, so the process stays alive.

concepts.name: Modules: ES modules vs CommonJS
concepts.summary: Node supports ES modules (import/export) and the older CommonJS (require). Learn how Node picks one and how the two work together.
concepts.why: Every Node file is one or the other, and mixing them up is the most common cause of confusing errors at startup.
concepts.body:
Node has two module systems, because it existed before JavaScript had a standard one:

- **ES modules (ESM)** — the JavaScript standard you learned: `import` / `export` and top-level `await`. All imports are loaded before the file's own code starts.
- **CommonJS (CJS)** — Node's original system: `require()` and `module.exports`. Each `require` loads the file right there and waits for it: it is **synchronous**, meaning one step at a time, with nothing else happening until it's done.

New code should be ESM. Node decides the format file by file:

- `.mjs` files are always ESM, `.cjs` files always CommonJS.
- `.js` files follow the nearest `package.json`, the project's settings file (next lesson). If it says `"type": "module"`, `.js` files are ESM; with no `type` setting (or `"commonjs"`), they are CommonJS. Node 22 can also guess from the code itself, but saying it explicitly is clearer.

Import built-in modules with the `node:` prefix — `import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises"` — so they can never be confused with a **package** (a bundle of code someone has published for others to install) that happens to have the same name.

ESM rules that trip people up:

- Imports of your own files need the **file extension**, the ending after the dot: `import { add } from "./math.js"`.
- `require`, `__dirname` and `__filename` don't exist. Use `import.meta.dirname` (the folder this file is in) and `import.meta.filename` instead.
- Importing a JSON file needs an extra note: `import data from "./data.json" with { type: "json" }`.

Mixing the two: an ES module can `import` a CommonJS file, whose `module.exports` arrives as the default export. The other direction is harder. Since Node 22.12, `require()` can load an ES module as long as it doesn't use top-level `await`. Otherwise use dynamic `import()`, a function form of import that works in both systems and returns a promise.

Prefer **named exports** for most things: when you rename one, your editor can update every place that uses it, and its name pops up in suggestions as you type.
takeaways: `"type": "module"` in package.json makes `.js` files ES modules
Use `node:` for built-ins and include file extensions when importing your own files
`import.meta.dirname` replaces `__dirname` in ES modules
Dynamic `import()` works everywhere; `require()` of an ES module only without top-level await
pitfalls: Writing `import x from './util'` without `.js` — ESM does not guess extensions.
Using `__dirname` in an ES module and getting a ReferenceError.

quiz.q: A package.json has no "type" field. How does Node treat app.js containing require() calls?
options: It refuses to run without a type field
quiz.explain: Without "type": "module", .js files default to CommonJS.

quiz.q: In an ES module, how do you get the directory of the current file?
quiz.explain: import.meta.dirname is the ESM equivalent; process.cwd() is where the process was started, which may differ.

concepts.name: npm and package.json
concepts.summary: Start a project with npm, add other people's packages to it, and learn what the package.json file records.
concepts.why: Almost every Node project starts with a package.json file and uses packages downloaded with npm.
concepts.body:
**npm** (Node Package Manager) is installed along with Node. A **package manager** installs and updates other people's code for you. It does two jobs. It downloads packages — usually **libraries**, ready-made code you call from your own — from the **npm registry**, a huge public website where anyone can publish them. And it runs your project's scripts.

A project is simply a folder with a **package.json** file in it: a JSON file that describes the project. Create one with `npm init -y`. The settings you'll touch most:

- `name`, `version` — the project's identity.
- `type` — set it to `"module"` to use ES modules.
- `scripts` — named commands, like `"dev": "node --watch src/server.js"`. Run one with `npm run dev`; `npm test` and `npm start` are shortcuts.
- `dependencies` — the packages your code needs to run. Each is a **dependency** of your project.
- `devDependencies` — tools needed only while writing the code: test tools, TypeScript, or a **linter** (a tool that points out likely mistakes).
- `engines` — which Node versions you support, e.g. `">=22"`.

Installing:

```bash
npm install express          # adds to dependencies
npm install -D eslint        # adds to devDependencies
npm uninstall express
npx eslint .                 # run a package's command-line tool
```

Installed packages land in a folder called **node_modules**. You never edit it, and you don't save it in **version control** — a system such as git that keeps every version of your code (with git, list it in `.gitignore`), because `npm install` can always recreate it from package.json. When you import a package by name, Node looks for it there.

Many packages include a **command-line tool**: a program you run by typing in a terminal. Inside your scripts, npm finds the project's own copy automatically, so `"lint": "eslint ."` runs the eslint installed in this project. Outside scripts, **npx** does the same: `npx eslint .`. Every developer on the project gets the same version.

Avoid `npm install -g` (a global install, for the whole computer) for project tools: the project would then quietly depend on something only your machine has. Keep them in `devDependencies` instead. Global installs are fine for personal tools you use everywhere.
concepts.code:
# Start a project and add a dependency
mkdir hello-api && cd hello-api
npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module
npm pkg set scripts.dev="node --watch server.js" scripts.test="node --test"
npm install express
npm install -D @types/node

# package.json now contains (abridged):
# {
#   "name": "hello-api",
#   "type": "module",
#   "scripts": { "dev": "node --watch server.js", "test": "node --test" },
#   "dependencies": { "express": "^5.1.0" },
#   "devDependencies": { "@types/node": "^22.10.0" }
# }

npm run dev        # or: node --run dev
npx eslint --version
takeaways: package.json describes the project: type, scripts and dependencies
`dependencies` are needed to run; `devDependencies` only while developing
Never edit node_modules or save it in version control; `npx` runs a project's installed tools
pitfalls: Installing project tools globally, so the project silently depends on your machine.

quiz.q: A test framework your code only uses during development should be installed with…
quiz.explain: -D records it under devDependencies, so installs for the live app can skip it.

concepts.name: Versions, lockfiles and npm ci
concepts.summary: Read version ranges like ^1.4.2, understand package-lock.json, and install exactly the same packages every time with npm ci.
concepts.why: Installing exactly the same versions everywhere prevents "works on my machine" bugs and surprises when a package your packages use gets updated.
concepts.body:
Each release of an npm package has a three-part version number, `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, following a rule called **semantic versioning** (semver). A major bump (2.0.0 → 3.0.0) may break code that uses the package; a minor bump adds features without breaking anything; a patch only fixes bugs.

In `package.json` you don't name one exact version but a **range** of acceptable ones:

- `^1.4.2` — any `1.x.y` at or above 1.4.2 (the default npm writes). For `0.x` versions the caret is stricter: `^0.4.2` means `>=0.4.2 <0.5.0`.
- `~1.4.2` — patch updates only: `>=1.4.2 <1.5.0`.
- `1.4.2` — exactly that version.

Ranges mean two installs a month apart could get different versions — including of the packages your packages depend on, which you never listed yourself. That's why npm writes **package-lock.json**, a **lock file**: it records the exact version and download address of every installed package, plus a **hash** of each one (a fingerprint of its contents, so a tampered download is caught). Save it in version control next to package.json.

Two install commands, two purposes:

- `npm install` — reads the ranges, may pick newer versions and update the lock file. Use it when adding or upgrading packages.
- `npm ci` — installs exactly what the lock file says, deletes node_modules first, and fails if package.json and the lock file disagree. Use it on build servers and anywhere installs must be repeatable.

To maintain dependencies:

- `npm outdated` lists packages with newer versions.
- `npm update` upgrades within your ranges; a major upgrade needs `npm install pkg@latest` and reading the package's list of changes.
- `npm ls pkg` shows which of your packages pulled `pkg` in.
- `npm audit` reports known **vulnerabilities** — security holes — in your packages.

Every dependency is code that runs with all the same powers as your own program. Prefer fewer, well-maintained packages, and check how widely used and actively maintained one is before adding it.
concepts.code:
# package.json ranges
#   "express": "^5.1.0"   -> 5.1.0 up to (not including) 6.0.0
#   "zod":     "~3.24.1"  -> 3.24.x only
#   "uuid":    "11.0.3"   -> exactly 11.0.3

npm install            # resolve ranges, update package-lock.json if needed
git add package.json package-lock.json

# On build servers: exact, clean, fails on mismatch
npm ci

npm outdated           # what is behind?
npm install express@latest   # deliberate major upgrade
npm ls debug           # which packages pull in 'debug'?
npm audit              # known vulnerabilities
takeaways: `^` allows minor and patch updates, `~` only patches
Save package-lock.json in version control; it pins every installed package, even indirect ones
Use `npm ci` for repeatable installs
pitfalls: Deleting package-lock.json to "fix" an install, which silently upgrades the whole tree.

quiz.q: package.json says "lib": "^2.3.0". Which version could npm install install?
quiz.explain: The caret allows any 2.x at or above 2.3.0, so 2.9.1 fits; 3.0.0 is a new major.

quiz.q: Why use npm ci rather than npm install on an automated build server?
options: It installs exactly the lockfile's versions and fails on mismatch
It is the only command that downloads from the registry
It upgrades packages to their latest versions
quiz.explain: npm ci gives a clean, reproducible install from the lockfile and errors if the lockfile is out of sync.

concepts.name: Reading and writing files with fs
concepts.summary: Use node:fs/promises with await to read, write and list files and folders.
concepts.why: Settings files, saved reports, records of what a program did — sooner or later almost every Node program reads or writes files.
concepts.body:
The built-in `node:fs` module (fs stands for **file system**, the way a computer organises files into folders) offers each operation in three styles: with callbacks (`fs.readFile(path, cb)`), synchronous (`fs.readFileSync`), and with promises. In everyday code use the promise style from **`node:fs/promises`** with `await`.

The everyday functions:

- `readFile(path, "utf8")` — the whole file as a string. Leave out `"utf8"` and you get a **Buffer** of raw **bytes** (the numbers 0–255 every file is really made of) instead.
- `writeFile(path, data)` — create or replace a file; `appendFile` adds to the end.
- `readdir(dir, { withFileTypes: true })` — a folder's entries, each with `isFile()` / `isDirectory()`; add `recursive: true` to include subfolders.
- `mkdir(dir, { recursive: true })` — creates the folder and any missing parents, and doesn't fail if it already exists.
- `stat(path)` — size, when it last changed, and whether it is a file or folder.
- `rm(path, { recursive: true, force: true })` — delete a file or a whole folder.
- `rename`, `copyFile`, `cp` (copy a folder), `access`.

Failures reject with an error whose `code` says what went wrong: `ENOENT` (no such file), `EACCES` (no permission), `EEXIST` (already exists), `EISDIR` (it's a folder). Check `err.code` rather than the message text.

Don't call `access()` or `stat()` to check whether a file exists before opening it: another process can create or delete it in between. Just try the operation and handle `ENOENT`.

The synchronous `*Sync` functions make your whole program wait until they finish; while one runs, Node can't do anything else, not even answer another visitor. They're fine in a short script or for loading settings once at startup, but never in code that runs for every incoming web request.

`readFile` loads the whole file into **memory** at once. For huge files, or files you process line by line, Node has **streams**, which handle data piece by piece (a later lesson).

Finally, a **relative path** like `"data.txt"` (one that doesn't start from the top folder) is looked up from the folder you started Node in, not the folder your script lives in. The code below builds paths from `import.meta.dirname` to stay safe; the next lesson explains why.
takeaways: Use `node:fs/promises` with await in everyday code
Handle errors by `err.code` (ENOENT, EACCES...); don't check existence first
Sync functions freeze the whole program — use them only in scripts and at startup
pitfalls: Using relative paths and being surprised when the script is run from another folder.
Reading huge files with readFile instead of streaming them.

quiz.q: You want to load settings.json but use defaults if it doesn't exist. What's the robust approach?
options: Call stat in a loop until the file appears
Call readFile and handle an error with code ENOENT
Use readFileSync each time a web request arrives
quiz.explain: Just try the read and handle ENOENT; a separate check can be out of date by the time you read.

concepts.name: Paths, URLs and the os module
concepts.summary: Build file paths that work on every system with node:path, turn file URLs into paths, and ask about the machine with node:os.
concepts.why: Paths glued together by hand break on Windows and when a script is started from another folder.
concepts.body:
A **file path** is a file's address: the folders you pass through to reach it, like `/home/ada/app/data.json`. Windows writes them differently (`C:\Users\ada\app\data.json`), so never glue paths together with `+ "/" +`. The `node:path` module knows each system's rules:

- `path.join("a", "b", "../c.txt")` → `a/c.txt` — joins pieces and tidies up `..` ("go up one folder") and doubled slashes.
- `path.resolve("data", "x.json")` → an **absolute path**, one that starts from the very top folder, such as `/home/ada/data/x.json`.
- `path.dirname`, `path.basename(p, ".js")` and `path.extname` take a path apart; `path.parse` returns all the parts as an object.
- `path.relative(from, to)` — how to get from one place to another.
- `path.sep` is `/` on macOS and Linux and `\` on Windows; `path.posix` always uses `/`.

The crucial question is where a **relative path** — one like `data/x.json` that doesn't start from the top — is looked up. The answer: from the **working directory**, the folder you were in when you started Node, which `process.cwd()` returns. That is not necessarily the folder your script lives in.

To find a file next to your own module, wherever Node was started from, build the path from the module's own folder: `path.join(import.meta.dirname, "templates", "email.html")`.

ES modules also identify themselves with a **file URL** — `import.meta.url`, e.g. `file:///home/me/app/main.js`, the same address style a browser uses. Most `fs` functions accept a `URL` directly, and `node:url` converts both ways with `fileURLToPath` and `pathToFileURL`. `new URL("./data.json", import.meta.url)` is a neat way to point at a file next to yours.

The `node:os` module answers questions about the machine: `os.availableParallelism()` (how many tasks the **processor** — the chip that carries out programs — can run at the same moment), `os.tmpdir()` (a folder for temporary files), `os.homedir()`, `os.EOL` (the characters that end a line), `os.totalmem()` / `os.freemem()` and `os.platform()`.
takeaways: Use `path.join` / `path.resolve`, never string concatenation
Relative paths are looked up from `process.cwd()`, not the module's folder
Anchor on `import.meta.dirname` or `new URL(..., import.meta.url)`
pitfalls: Using `path.join` to build URLs on Windows — it inserts backslashes; use `path.posix` or `URL`.

quiz.q: A script in /app/tools/gen.js reads path.resolve("tpl.txt"). The user runs `node tools/gen.js` from /app. Which file is read?
options: It throws because the path is relative
quiz.explain: path.resolve uses the current working directory (/app), not the script's folder.

concepts.name: The process object and exit codes
concepts.summary: Use the global process object to read arguments, write output, report success or failure with exit codes, and react to stop requests.
concepts.why: Programs are often started by other programs; exit codes and stop requests are how yours cooperates with them.
concepts.body:
`process` is a global object describing your running Node process. Its most useful parts follow.

**Arguments.** The words typed after the command — `3` and `4` in `node sum.js 3 4` — are **command-line arguments**. `process.argv` is an array of them as strings: `[0]` is the path to Node itself, `[1]` your script, and the rest are yours, so `process.argv.slice(2)` gives `["3", "4"]`.

**Output channels.** Every process has two of them. **Standard output** (stdout) is for results; `console.log` writes there. **Standard error** (stderr) is for messages and problems; `console.error` writes there. Both normally appear in the terminal, but they can be sent to different places.

That matters because of **pipes**: in a terminal, `node sum.js 3 4 | other-program` sends your stdout straight into another program as its input — its **standard input** (stdin). Keep stdout for results only, and your program fits into such chains. `process.stdout`, `process.stderr` and `process.stdin` let you use the channels directly.

**Other details.** `process.cwd()` gives the folder Node was started from, `process.env` holds settings passed in from outside (next lesson), and `process.pid`, `process.platform`, `process.version` and `process.uptime()` describe the process.

**Exit codes.** When a program ends, it reports a number to whoever started it: 0 means success, anything else means failure. Scripts and automated checks look at it to decide whether to carry on. Node exits with 0 when it has nothing left to do, and with 1 when an error is never caught.

To report failure yourself, prefer `process.exitCode = 1` and let the program finish on its own. `process.exit(code)` stops *immediately*: output still on its way to the screen or a file can be cut off.

**Stop requests.** Other programs can ask yours to stop by sending a **process signal**, a short notice delivered by the operating system. Pressing Ctrl+C in the terminal sends one called **SIGINT**.

Servers that run your app send **SIGTERM**, the polite "please shut down". Without a handler, Node exits at once. With `process.on("SIGTERM", ...)` you can finish current work first.

The `"exit"` event fires as the process ends, but only code that finishes immediately runs inside it — you can't `await` there. For cleanup that needs to wait, handle the signal instead.
takeaways: `process.argv.slice(2)` are your arguments
Prefer `process.exitCode = n` over `process.exit(n)`
Results to stdout, messages to stderr
Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to stop cleanly
pitfalls: Calling `process.exit()` right after writing output, cutting it off when it is piped to another program.

quiz.q: Why is process.exitCode = 1 usually better than process.exit(1)?
options: exitCode lets pending I/O finish before the process ends
exitCode also stops any other programs you started
quiz.explain: process.exit() terminates immediately, potentially dropping buffered output; exitCode just sets the code used at a natural exit.

concepts.name: Environment variables and .env files
concepts.summary: Read settings from process.env, load them from a .env file with --env-file, and check them once at startup.
concepts.why: Keeping settings and passwords outside the code lets the same program run on your laptop and on the live server.
concepts.body:
Some settings change depending on where your program runs: the address of the **database** it stores its data in, the **API keys** (password-like strings) it sends when calling other services, how much detail it should print. They don't belong in the code.

Instead they're passed in as **environment variables**: named text settings that the operating system hands to a program when it starts. Node exposes them as `process.env`, a plain object whose values are **always strings** (or `undefined` if not set).

On macOS or Linux you can set them right before the command:

```bash
PORT=8080 LOG_LEVEL=debug node server.js
```

During development you usually keep them in a **.env file**, a text file of `NAME=value` lines. Node 22 reads it itself:

- `node --env-file=.env server.js` — fails if the file is missing; `--env-file-if-exists` doesn't.
- Pass the flag several times; later files win over earlier ones.
- Variables already set outside win over the file, so a stray `.env` can't change the live server's settings.
- From code: `process.loadEnvFile(".env")`.

A .env file usually holds **secrets**: passwords and keys nobody else should see. So never share it or save it with your code (with git, list it in `.gitignore`). Instead, share a `.env.example` with dummy values, so others know which variables to set.

Read and check all settings **once, at startup**, in one module. Convert types yourself — `Number(process.env.PORT)`, `process.env.DEBUG === "true"` — because `"false"` is a non-empty string and therefore truthy. If something required is missing, stop with a clear message: a crash at startup beats an `undefined` password discovered at 3 a.m.

`NODE_ENV=production` is a common convention: many **packages** (ready-made code you install) check it to switch off developer-only features. **Production** means the live system real users rely on. Set it there, but don't use it as your only switch; specific variables are clearer.
takeaways: `process.env` values are strings or undefined — convert them yourself
`node --env-file=.env` loads a .env file, no extra package needed
Check all settings once at startup and stop early if one is missing
pitfalls: Sharing a `.env` file that holds real secrets, for example by saving it in git.
Writing `if (process.env.FEATURE)` and turning the feature on when it is set to "false".

quiz.q: process.env.ENABLE_CACHE is set to the string "false". What does `if (process.env.ENABLE_CACHE)` do?
options: Runs the block, because a non-empty string is truthy
quiz.explain: Environment values are strings; "false" is a non-empty string and therefore truthy.

concepts.name: Command-line arguments and user input
concepts.summary: Read flags with util.parseArgs, ask questions with readline/promises, and accept input piped in from another program.
concepts.why: Small command-line tools — programs you use by typing in a terminal — are one of the most common things people write in Node.
concepts.body:
`process.argv` gives you plain strings. Real tools take flags like `--max 5` or `-i`. The built-in **`util.parseArgs`** reads them for you, handling `--name value`, `--name=value`, one-letter short forms and on/off switches:

- Declare `options` with a `type` (`"string"` or `"boolean"`), and optionally `short`, `default` and `multiple`.
- Set `allowPositionals: true` to also accept plain words that aren't flags.
- Unknown flags throw an error by default (`strict: true`), so typos don't slip through.

For interactive questions, use `node:readline/promises`. Create a reader with `createInterface({ input: process.stdin, output: process.stdout })`, then `await rl.question("Name? ")`, and call `rl.close()` when done — an open reader keeps the process alive, waiting for more typing.

Tools that fit into pipes also read standard input: `cat data.txt | node count.js`. `process.stdin` delivers that input as a **stream**, piece by piece as it arrives, so the easiest way to read it is `readline.createInterface({ input: process.stdin })` and `for await (const line of rl)`, which gives you one line at a time. `process.stdin.isTTY` is true when a person is typing rather than data being piped in.

For output: `console.log` for results, `console.error` for messages. `util.styleText("red", "error")` adds colour without installing anything, and recent Node versions leave the colour out automatically when output isn't going to a terminal. `console.table` prints an array of objects as a neat table.

When a tool grows several **subcommands** (like `git commit` and `git push`), help pages and the like, a **package** — ready-made code someone has published — such as `commander` can help. Many tools never need more than `parseArgs`.
takeaways: `util.parseArgs` handles flags, short forms and plain words without extra packages
`readline/promises` for questions; close the reader when finished
`for await` over a readline reader reads piped input line by line
pitfalls: Forgetting `rl.close()`, so the process hangs waiting for input.

quiz.q: With parseArgs in its default strict mode, what happens when the user passes an undeclared --verbose flag?
options: It is stored in values.verbose as true
quiz.explain: strict mode (the default) rejects unknown options so typos are caught.

concepts.name: Async patterns in Node
concepts.summary: From callbacks to promises: convert old functions, run work side by side, add time limits, and cancel with AbortSignal.
concepts.why: Real services juggle many slow operations; running them in the right order, side by side, and cancelling them when needed is the job.
concepts.body:
Node's original convention is the **error-first callback**: the last argument is a function called as `cb(err, result)`. You will still meet it in older code. Every built-in module now has a promise form (`node:fs/promises`, `node:timers/promises`, `node:dns/promises`, `node:stream/promises`), and `util.promisify(fn)` turns any error-first function into one that returns a promise.

With promises, the main skill is choosing between **sequential** (one after another) and running things side by side so their waiting overlaps — **concurrency**:

- `await a(); await b();` — b starts only after a finishes. Right when b needs a's result.
- `await Promise.all([a(), b()])` — both run at once; it fails as soon as one rejects.
- `Promise.allSettled` when you want every outcome, even failures.

Unlimited concurrency is its own bug: `Promise.all(urls.map((u) => fetch(u)))` over 10,000 URLs opens ten thousand network connections at once. Process big lists in **batches** — a few items at a time — or with a small pool.

**Cancellation** uses **AbortController**, the same object browsers have. Pass its `signal` to `fetch`, `fs.readFile`, `setTimeout` from `timers/promises`, `events.once` and others; calling `controller.abort()` makes them reject with an `AbortError`. For deadlines, `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` gives you a signal that aborts by itself after that many milliseconds — a **timeout** — and `AbortSignal.any([a, b])` combines several.

`node:timers/promises` gives awaitable timers: `await setTimeout(500)` pauses for half a second, and `for await (const _ of setInterval(1000))` loops once a second.

Finally, never leave a promise floating. A rejected promise nobody awaits becomes an **unhandled rejection**, which crashes Node by default. If you deliberately start something without waiting for it, attach a `.catch()`.
takeaways: `util.promisify` converts error-first callback functions
Independent work: `Promise.all`; dependent work: one `await` after another
Limit concurrency for big lists
Cancel with AbortController; set deadlines with `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)`
pitfalls: Awaiting inside a for loop for independent requests, making them wait for each other for no reason.
Firing a promise without await or .catch, causing an unhandled rejection crash.

quiz.q: You must call getUser(id) and getOrders(id); neither needs the other's result. What's best?
quiz.explain: Promise.all starts both at once and waits for both, halving the wall-clock time.

quiz.q: How do you give a fetch call a 2-second deadline in Node 22?
quiz.explain: fetch has no timeout option; an AbortSignal that aborts itself after 2000 ms is the standard way.

concepts.name: Events and EventEmitter
concepts.summary: Emit and listen to named events with EventEmitter, the building block behind Node's servers, streams and network connections.
concepts.why: Much of Node's built-in code is built on EventEmitter, so you need it to understand servers, streams and processes.
concepts.body:
An **EventEmitter** is an object that announces named events and lets other code subscribe with listener functions — like signing up for a shop's "back in stock" email. Node's servers, network connections, streams, and `process` itself are all EventEmitters.

The core methods:

- `emitter.on(name, listener)` — call `listener` every time `name` is emitted; `once` only for the next one.
- `emitter.emit(name, ...args)` — call every listener for `name`, in the order they were added, passing the args.
- `emitter.off(name, listener)` — remove a listener (you need the same function, not a copy).

Two facts matter more than the methods. First, **`emit` is synchronous**: every listener runs, one after another, before `emit` returns. A slow listener slows down whoever emitted; a listener that throws makes `emit` throw. If a listener has slow work to do, it should start it asynchronously and return.

Second, the event named **`"error"` is special**. If an emitter emits `"error"` and nobody listens, Node throws the error and — unless something catches it — the process crashes. Always attach an `error` listener to network connections, streams and anything else that can fail.

Bridging to async/await:

- `await once(emitter, "ready")` (from `node:events`) waits for a single event, and rejects if `"error"` fires first.
- `for await (const [msg] of on(emitter, "message"))` runs the loop body once per event.

To write your own, extend `EventEmitter` in a class and call `this.emit(...)`. Node prints a **MaxListenersExceededWarning** when more than 10 listeners attach to one event. That usually means a **memory leak**: code adds a listener for every request and never removes it, so memory use grows forever. Raise the limit with `setMaxListeners` only if it is genuinely intended.

Browsers' `EventTarget` also exists in Node; use it when you want code that also runs in browsers, but most Node modules use EventEmitter.
takeaways: `emit` calls listeners synchronously, in order
An unhandled `'error'` event throws and usually crashes the process
`events.once` / `events.on` bridge events to async/await
pitfalls: Adding a listener each time a request arrives and never removing it (memory leak + MaxListeners warning).

quiz.q: An emitter emits 'error' with no 'error' listener attached. What happens?
options: The error is thrown, typically crashing the process
Node logs a warning and continues
The error is queued until a listener is added
quiz.explain: 'error' is special: without a listener, emit throws the error.

concepts.name: Streams: reading and writing in chunks
concepts.summary: Process data piece by piece with readable, writable and transform streams, and connect them safely with pipeline().
concepts.why: Streams let you handle files and network data far bigger than memory while using only a little memory.
concepts.body:
A stream delivers data in chunks over time instead of all at once. There are four kinds:

- **Readable** — a source: `fs.createReadStream`, an incoming HTTP request on a server, `process.stdin`.
- **Writable** — a destination: `fs.createWriteStream`, an HTTP response, `process.stdout`.
- **Duplex** — both at once, independently, like a network connection (a **socket**).
- **Transform** — a duplex whose output is computed from its input, such as `zlib.createGzip()` (compression) or a parser for **CSV** files.

Copying a 5 GB log with `readFile` + `writeFile` needs 5 GB of memory; with streams it needs about 64 KB at a time.

The right way to connect streams is **`pipeline`** from `node:stream/promises`, which chains them like stations on a factory line:

```javascript
await pipeline(createReadStream("in.log"), createGzip(), createWriteStream("in.log.gz"));
```

It passes each stage's output to the next, reports an error from any stage, destroys all streams if one fails, and resolves when everything finishes. The older `a.pipe(b)` does none of that error handling: a failing source leaves the destination open, and the open file is never released.

Readable streams are async iterables, so the simplest way to consume one is `for await (const chunk of stream)`. Chunks are `Buffer`s unless you set a text **encoding** (`createReadStream(path, { encoding: "utf8" })`) or the stream is in **object mode**, where each chunk can be any JavaScript value.

To write your own transform, `new Transform({ transform(chunk, enc, cb) { cb(null, result) } })` works. Often simpler: pass an **async generator** function (`async function*`) as a pipeline stage. A generator can hand out many values, one at a time, with `yield`; this one receives the previous stage as something to loop over and yields its output.

Node also implements the browser's web streams (`ReadableStream`, used by `fetch` bodies); `Readable.fromWeb` and `Readable.toWeb` convert between the two.
takeaways: Streams move data in chunks, using little memory
Connect stages with `pipeline` from `node:stream/promises`, not `.pipe()`
Readable streams work with `for await`; async generators make easy transforms
pitfalls: Using `.pipe()` without error handling, leaving files open when a stage fails.
Assuming a chunk ends exactly at the end of a line or record.

quiz.q: What does stream.pipeline do that a.pipe(b).pipe(c) does not?
options: Makes the copy faster by using extra threads
Reads the whole input into memory first
Forwards errors from any stage and destroys all streams on failure
quiz.explain: pipeline handles errors and cleanup across all stages; .pipe() leaves that to you.

concepts.name: Building an HTTP server with node:http
concepts.summary: Create a web server with node:http: pick what to do for each request, read request bodies, set status and headers, and send responses.
concepts.why: Every Node web framework — a package that handles the routine parts of web apps, like Express — is a layer over this module; knowing it makes frameworks unmysterious.
concepts.body:
`http.createServer(handler)` returns a server that calls `handler(req, res)` for each request. `server.listen(3000)` starts accepting connections on **port** 3000 — a numbered door on the computer that network traffic is addressed to, so one machine can run many services.

- `req` is an **IncomingMessage** (a readable stream): `req.method`, `req.url` (the path plus query string, e.g. `/users?page=2`) and `req.headers`, whose names are **lower-case**.
- `res` is a **ServerResponse** (a writable stream): set `res.statusCode` or call `res.writeHead(status, headers)`, `res.setHeader(name, value)`, write with `res.write(chunk)`, and always finish with `res.end(body)`.

Parse the URL with the standard `URL` class: `new URL(req.url, "http://localhost")` gives you `pathname` and `searchParams`.

The **request body** — the data the caller sends along, such as a submitted form or JSON — isn't parsed for you; it arrives as a stream. Collect it with `for await (const chunk of req)`, join the Buffers, then `JSON.parse`. Cap the size so nobody can send you a gigabyte, and answer 400 on invalid JSON.

Things the raw module leaves to you, which frameworks provide: **routing** (picking the right code for each URL and method), body parsing, content types, cookies and error handling. Note also:

- Every code path must end the response, or the caller waits until it gives up.
- An error thrown inside an `async` handler is an unhandled rejection — wrap the handler in try/catch and answer 500.
- Headers must be set before the first `write`; after that `res.headersSent` is true and setting one throws.

`node:https` works the same way but encrypts traffic with **TLS**, the technology behind the padlock in your browser; `node:http2` supports HTTP/2. On a live server you'll often run plain HTTP behind a **load balancer**, a front server that handles the encryption and spreads traffic across copies of your app.
takeaways: `req` is a readable stream, `res` a writable stream
You parse URLs and bodies yourself, and must always call `res.end()`
Header names in `req.headers` are lower-case
Catch errors in async handlers and answer with a status code
pitfalls: Forgetting to end the response on one code path, leaving the client hanging.
Reading request bodies without a size limit.

quiz.q: A client sends JSON in a POST. Where is it in a plain node:http handler?
options: In the req stream; you must read and parse it
quiz.explain: node:http doesn't parse bodies; req is a readable stream you consume (frameworks add req.body).

concepts.name: Making HTTP requests with fetch
concepts.summary: Call other web services with the built-in fetch: check the status, send JSON, set time limits, stream responses and reuse connections.
concepts.why: Talking to other services is part of nearly every backend — the server side of an app — and fetch is now the standard way.
concepts.body:
Node 22 has a global, browser-compatible **`fetch`**, built on **undici**, the HTTP client library inside Node. No extra packages such as `axios` are needed.

The most important rule: **fetch only rejects when the network fails**, not on HTTP errors. A 404 or 500 resolves normally with `res.ok === false`. Always check `res.ok` (or `res.status`) before using the body.

Sending JSON means doing it yourself:

```javascript
await fetch(url, {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify(data),
});
```

Reading the body: `await res.json()`, `res.text()`, `res.arrayBuffer()`, or `res.body`, a web `ReadableStream` you can loop over with `for await`, or convert with `Readable.fromWeb` to write it to a file. A body can be read only once. If you don't need it, call `await res.body?.cancel()` so the connection can be reused.

There is **no default timeout** per request; pass `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000)`. A request stopped this way rejects with an error named `TimeoutError` (from `timeout`) or `AbortError` (from `abort()`).

Behind the scenes undici keeps a few connections to each site open and reuses them (a **connection pool**), so repeated calls to the same service are cheap. For advanced tuning — pool size, going through a **proxy** server, custom encryption settings — install the `undici` package and pass a `dispatcher`.

**Retries** — trying again after a failure — are your job. Only retry **idempotent** requests, where doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once: GET, PUT and DELETE, on network errors and on 502, 503 or 504.

Wait longer after each failure (**exponential backoff**: 1 s, then 2 s, then 4 s…) up to a limit, and if a 429 response includes a `Retry-After` header, wait that long.

`FormData`, `Blob`, `Headers`, `Request` and `Response` are available everywhere too, as in the browser, so file uploads and fake responses for tests work the same way.
takeaways: fetch resolves on HTTP errors — check `res.ok`
Use `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` for deadlines
Bodies are streams, readable once; cancel unused ones
pitfalls: Calling `res.json()` on an error response and getting a confusing parse error instead of the status.

quiz.q: fetch() to an endpoint returns HTTP 503. What happens?
options: The promise resolves; res.ok is false and res.status is 503
The promise rejects with a TypeError
Node emits an 'error' event on process
quiz.explain: fetch only rejects for network-level failures; HTTP error statuses resolve normally.

concepts.name: Error handling in Node applications
concepts.summary: Distinguish operational from programmer errors, use error codes and causes, and handle uncaught exceptions and rejections.
concepts.why: How a service fails decides whether an incident is a logged warning or a crashed, corrupted process.
concepts.body:
Two kinds of error need different treatment:

- **Operational errors** are expected failures of a correct program: file not found, connection refused, invalid user input, a timeout. Handle them — try again, answer with a 4xx status, fall back to defaults.
- **Programmer errors** are bugs: `undefined is not a function`, an argument of the wrong type. You can't sensibly recover; log it, crash, and let a supervisor (a program that watches yours) restart the process.

Node's errors carry a stable **`code`** property (`ENOENT`, `ECONNREFUSED`, `ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE`). Branch on `err.code`, never on the message text, which can change between versions. Do the same in your own code: subclass `Error`, set `name` and a `code`, and add properties with useful details.

When you catch an error and throw a new one, keep the original with **`cause`**: `throw new Error("loading user 42 failed", { cause: err })`. **Logs** (the notes a program writes about what it did) and `util.inspect` then show both errors' **stack traces**: the list of function calls that led to each error.

Async rules:

- `try/catch` only catches a rejection if you `await` the promise inside the `try`.
- A promise rejection nobody handles triggers `unhandledRejection`; since Node 15 the default is to **crash** with **exit code** 1 (the number a program reports when it ends; anything but 0 means failure).
- A thrown error that escapes everything triggers `uncaughtException` and also crashes.

You can listen for both on `process`, but use them only to **log and exit** (`process.exit(1)` once your logs are written). After an uncaught exception, the process may be in a broken state — half-written data, resources still held — so carrying on is dangerous. Run under something that restarts you, such as **systemd** on a Linux server or your hosting platform's restart setting.

Finally, throw `Error` objects, not strings: only errors have stack traces.
takeaways: Handle operational errors; crash and restart on programmer errors
Branch on `err.code`, wrap with `{ cause }` to keep context
Unhandled rejections crash Node by default
Use uncaught handlers only to log and exit
pitfalls: Catching `uncaughtException` and continuing to serve requests from a corrupted state.
`try { promise } catch` without `await`, so the rejection escapes.

quiz.q: Which error should a service typically handle and keep running?
options: TypeError: user.name is not a function
RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
An ECONNREFUSED when calling a downstream API
quiz.explain: A refused connection is an operational error you can retry or report; the others are bugs.

quiz.q: Why is checking err.code better than matching err.message?
options: Codes are stable API; messages may change between versions
Messages are not available on system errors
err.message is undefined for async errors
quiz.explain: Node documents error codes as stable, while message text is not guaranteed.

concepts.name: Debugging Node with the inspector
concepts.summary: Debug with --inspect and Chrome DevTools or VS Code: breakpoints, stepping through code, watching variables and debugging tests.
concepts.why: A real debugger — a tool that pauses your program so you can look inside — finds bugs faster than scattering console.log calls.
concepts.body:
Node includes the **inspector**, a debugging service that a debugger connects to — the same one Chrome uses for web pages. Start your program with a flag:

- `node --inspect app.js` — runs normally and waits for a debugger to connect on `127.0.0.1:9229` (**port** 9229 on your own machine).
- `node --inspect-brk app.js` — pauses before the first line, so you can set breakpoints in code that runs at startup.
- `node --inspect-wait app.js` — waits for a debugger to connect, then runs.

Then connect a debugger:

- **Chrome DevTools**: open `chrome://inspect` and click "Open dedicated DevTools for Node". You get your source files, **breakpoints** (lines where the program will pause), a console running inside your program, and Memory and Performance tabs.
- **VS Code**: its JavaScript Debug Terminal connects automatically to any `node` you start in it, or you can write a launch configuration. Click next to a line number to set a breakpoint.

While paused you can step over, into or out of functions, and look at the **call stack** — the chain of function calls that led to this line, including which `await` you came from. You can add watch expressions, and set conditional breakpoints (pause only when an expression is true) or **logpoints** (print a message without pausing). A `debugger;` statement in code acts as a breakpoint when a debugger is connected.

Never open the inspector to the network: `--inspect=0.0.0.0` lets anyone who can reach that port run any code inside your process. To debug another machine, keep the default — reachable only from that machine itself, its **localhost** — and connect through an **SSH** tunnel, an encrypted connection forwarded from your computer.

Other helpful tools: `node inspect app.js` is a debugger inside the terminal; `NODE_DEBUG=http,net` turns on internal debug messages from built-in modules; `console.trace()` prints the current stack; `--enable-source-maps` makes stack traces point to your original TypeScript lines. For tests, `node --inspect-brk --test` lets you step through a failing test.
concepts.code:
# Pause at the first line and attach Chrome DevTools (chrome://inspect)
node --inspect-brk server.js

# Debug a single failing test file
node --inspect-brk --test test/user.test.js

# Readable stack traces for transpiled code
node --enable-source-maps dist/server.js

# Internal debug logging from core modules
NODE_DEBUG=http,net node server.js

# Remote host: keep the inspector on localhost and tunnel it
ssh -L 9229:127.0.0.1:9229 user@server   # then attach to localhost:9229
takeaways: `--inspect` / `--inspect-brk` turn on the debugger on port 9229
Connect via chrome://inspect or VS Code's JavaScript Debug Terminal
Conditional breakpoints and logpoints save edit-and-restart cycles
Never open the inspector to the network
pitfalls: Running `--inspect=0.0.0.0` on a server, which lets anyone run code in your process.

quiz.q: You need to break inside code that runs during module loading. Which flag fits?
quiz.explain: --inspect-brk pauses before user code starts, giving you time to set breakpoints.

concepts.name: Testing with node:test
concepts.summary: Write and run tests with Node's built-in test runner and assert module, including stand-in functions, async tests and coverage.
concepts.why: Built-in testing means zero-dependency, fast tests that work in every Node project.
concepts.body:
Node ships a complete **test runner** — a tool that finds your test files, runs them and reports what passed — in **`node:test`**. Most projects need no Jest or Mocha.

- Organise tests with `describe(name, fn)` and `it(name, fn)` (or `test`). Async functions just work: the test waits for the promise.
- Hooks run code around tests: `before`, `after`, `beforeEach`, `afterEach`.
- Modifiers: `it.skip`, `it.todo`, `it.only` (run with `--test-only`).

**Assertions** — checks that fail the test when something is wrong — come from **`node:assert/strict`**: `equal` (strict `===`), `deepEqual` (same structure and values), `ok`, `throws` for synchronous code and **`await assert.rejects(promise, matcher)`** for async code. Always use the `strict` variant; the old one uses loose `==`.

Run tests with `node --test`. With no arguments it finds files named like `*.test.js` or `*-test.js`, plus files in `test/` folders, and runs each **file in its own process**, several at once. Useful flags:

- `--watch` reruns tests when files change.
- `--test-name-pattern="login"` runs only tests whose names match.
- `--experimental-test-coverage` shows which lines your tests ran.
- `--test-reporter=spec|dot|tap|junit` changes the output (junit is a format build servers understand).

**Mocks** — stand-in versions of real functions that record how they were called — are built in through `t.mock` / `mock`: `mock.fn()` creates a recording function, `mock.method(obj, "name", impl)` replaces a method and restores it after the test, and `mock.timers.enable()` fakes `setTimeout` and `Date` so time-dependent code runs instantly.

Good tests check behaviour: call the public function, or send a real request to your server, and check the outputs and side effects. Keep each test independent — create fresh state in `beforeEach` rather than relying on test order.
takeaways: `node --test` runs `*.test.js` files, each in its own process
Use `node:assert/strict`; `assert.rejects` for async errors
`mock.fn`, `mock.method` and `mock.timers` cover most mocking
pitfalls: Writing `assert.rejects(promise)` without `await`, so the test passes before the check runs.

quiz.q: Which assertion correctly checks that an async function rejects?
quiz.explain: assert.rejects awaits the promise and checks that it rejects; throws only sees synchronous throws.

concepts.name: Offloading CPU work to worker threads
concepts.summary: Run heavy calculations on worker threads so your main program stays responsive, passing data back and forth as messages.
concepts.why: A single slow calculation on the main thread freezes every request your server is handling.
concepts.body:
Node runs your JavaScript on one **thread** — one line of execution, doing one step at a time. That's perfect for I/O, because waiting doesn't occupy the thread. But a **CPU-bound** task, one limited by how fast the processor can calculate — resizing an image, parsing a huge JSON file, a long numeric loop — keeps the thread busy. Until it finishes the event loop is stuck: no other requests are served and no timers fire.

**`node:worker_threads`** runs JavaScript on extra threads. The thread your program starts on is the **main thread**; each **Worker** gets its own copy of the JavaScript engine (an **isolate**), its own event loop and its own modules. Workers don't share variables with the main thread; they talk by **messages**:

- Create one with `new Worker(new URL("./worker.js", import.meta.url), { workerData })`.
- In the worker, `workerData` holds the initial input, and `parentPort.postMessage(result)` sends results back.
- The parent listens for `"message"`, `"error"` (an uncaught exception in the worker) and `"exit"`.

Messages are copied with **structured clone**, a built-in deep copy that handles plain objects, arrays, Maps, Dates and typed arrays, but not functions or class methods. A large `ArrayBuffer` (a block of raw bytes) can be **transferred** instead of copied: it moves to the worker, with no copying.

Starting a worker takes a few milliseconds and several **megabytes** of memory, so don't start one per request. For frequent work, keep a **pool** of long-lived workers, about one per processor core (`os.availableParallelism()`); the `piscina` package does this well.

Workers are the wrong tool for I/O: the main thread already handles many I/O operations at once. Use them only when measuring shows that JavaScript calculation is the **bottleneck**, the slowest part that holds everything else back.

Some built-ins already do their heavy part on background threads when you call their async versions: `crypto.pbkdf2` (password **hashing**), `zlib` (compression) and `fs` use the small **thread pool** that **libuv**, Node's C library for talking to the operating system, keeps ready. Prefer those to writing your own workers.
takeaways: CPU-bound JavaScript blocks the event loop; workers run it on other threads
Workers share nothing by default and talk through copied messages
Reuse workers through a pool; never start one per request
pitfalls: Using worker threads for work that mostly waits on files or the network, adding cost with no benefit.

quiz.q: Which task benefits most from a worker thread?
options: Resizing a large image in pure JavaScript
Reading a config file at startup
quiz.explain: Image processing in plain JavaScript is CPU-bound; the others are I/O that Node already does concurrently.

concepts.name: Backpressure and custom streams
concepts.summary: Understand highWaterMark, write() returning false and 'drain', and build Transform streams that respect backpressure.
concepts.why: Ignoring backpressure is how a fast producer and slow consumer turn into an out-of-memory crash.
concepts.body:
Every stream has an internal **buffer** — a holding area for chunks waiting to be processed — whose target size is the **highWaterMark** (64 KiB for byte streams in Node 22, 16 objects in object mode). It is a threshold, not a hard limit, and it is how **backpressure** works: the mechanism by which a slow consumer tells a fast producer to wait.

On the writable side, `writable.write(chunk)` returns a boolean. `false` means "my buffer is above the highWaterMark — stop until I emit `'drain'`". The data is still accepted; nothing enforces the pause. Code that ignores the return value keeps buffering, and memory grows until the process dies.

```javascript
if (!out.write(chunk)) await once(out, "drain");
```

On the readable side, a stream reads ahead only until its buffer reaches the highWaterMark, then waits for the consumer. In a custom `Readable`, `push()` returning `false` is your signal to stop producing until `_read()` is called again.

The good news: **`pipeline()` and `for await` handle all of this for you.** `pipeline` pauses sources when destinations fill up; async iteration only pulls the next chunk when your loop body finishes. Manual `on("data")` handlers are where backpressure gets lost, because `'data'` keeps firing however slowly you process it.

When writing a `Transform`, call the callback only when you have finished with the chunk, push output with `this.push()`, and use `flush(callback)` to emit anything buffered at the end. Errors go to `callback(err)`, which destroys the stream and propagates through `pipeline`.

Tune `highWaterMark` deliberately: bigger buffers move more data per second in large copies, smaller ones use less memory per connection. Measure before changing it.
takeaways: `write()` returning false means wait for `'drain'`
`pipeline` and `for await` apply backpressure automatically
In Transforms, call the callback when done and use `flush` for trailing output
pitfalls: Writing in a loop and ignoring `write()`'s return value, buffering unbounded data.
Consuming with `on('data')` and slow async work, which defeats backpressure.

quiz.q: writable.write(chunk) returns false. What does that mean?
options: The chunk was rejected and must be resent
The buffer is above highWaterMark; pause until 'drain'
An error occurred and 'error' will follow
quiz.explain: The chunk was buffered, but the producer should stop writing until 'drain' fires.

concepts.name: The event loop phases and libuv
concepts.summary: Learn the event loop's phases, where nextTick, promises, setImmediate and timers run, and what libuv's thread pool does.
concepts.why: Explains surprising callback orders, starved I/O, and why some 'async' operations are slower than others.
concepts.body:
Node's event loop comes from **libuv**, the C library Node uses to talk to the operating system. It goes round and round through **phases**, each with a **queue** — a waiting line — of callbacks:

- **timers** — expired `setTimeout` / `setInterval` callbacks.
- **pending callbacks** — some system errors that were put off.
- **poll** — waits for new I/O events and runs their callbacks (data arriving on a connection, finished file reads). If nothing else is scheduled, the loop waits here.
- **check** — `setImmediate` callbacks.
- **close callbacks** — `'close'` events, for example of network connections.

Between every single callback, Node empties two higher-priority queues: first the **`process.nextTick`** queue, then the promise **microtask** queue (`then` callbacks, code after `await`). That is why a promise continuation always runs before the next timer, and why a `nextTick` callback that keeps scheduling another one (or an endless chain of resolved promises) can **starve** I/O completely: the loop never gets to it.

Practical consequences:

- Inside an I/O callback, `setImmediate` always runs before `setTimeout(fn, 0)`, because check comes right after poll. From the main module their order is not guaranteed.
- `setTimeout(fn, 10)` means "not before 10 ms", never "exactly at 10 ms".
- Prefer `queueMicrotask` or `setImmediate` over `process.nextTick` unless you specifically need to run before any other async work.

Network I/O uses the operating system's own non-blocking mechanisms (epoll, kqueue, IOCP) directly. But file reads, `dns.lookup` (turning a **domain name** into an address), and processor-heavy `crypto`/`zlib` work run on libuv's **thread pool**: a few background threads that take jobs from a queue. It has only **4 threads** by default (`UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`, max 1024, set before startup), so many simultaneous `fs` or `pbkdf2` calls wait in line there — a common hidden **bottleneck**.

Measure the loop's health with `perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay()`; a consistently high delay means something is **blocking** the thread.
takeaways: Phases: timers → pending → poll → check → close
nextTick then promise microtasks run between every callback
fs, dns.lookup, crypto and zlib use libuv's 4-thread pool by default
Endless nextTick or promise callbacks starve I/O
pitfalls: Using `process.nextTick` recursively and starving I/O.
Running hundreds of concurrent fs or crypto calls and blaming the disk for thread-pool queuing.

quiz.q: Inside an fs.readFile callback, you schedule setTimeout(a, 0) and setImmediate(b). Which runs first?
quiz.explain: After the poll phase the loop moves to check (setImmediate) before wrapping round to timers.

quiz.q: Your server makes many parallel crypto.pbkdf2 calls and latency climbs. Which setting is most relevant?
quiz.explain: Async pbkdf2 runs on libuv's thread pool, which defaults to 4 threads.

concepts.name: Worker pools, shared memory and cluster
concepts.summary: Use every processor core: pool worker threads, share memory between threads with SharedArrayBuffer, and run copies of a server with the cluster module.
concepts.why: One Node process uses one processor core for JavaScript; busy live servers usually need all of them.
concepts.body:
There are two ways to use more than one processor core from Node, and they solve different problems.

**Worker thread pools** speed up CPU-heavy *tasks* inside one process. Create N long-lived workers (N ≈ `os.availableParallelism()` minus one for the main thread), keep a waiting list of tasks, and hand each task to an idle worker. A pool must cope with a worker crashing (replace it, reject its task) and must support shutting down. `piscina` is the popular package for this.

To avoid copying large data:

- **Transfer** an `ArrayBuffer` (`postMessage(buf, [buf])`) — ownership moves, the sender's copy becomes unusable, nothing is copied.
- **Share** a **SharedArrayBuffer**: both threads see the same memory. Coordinate with `Atomics` (`Atomics.add`, `Atomics.wait` / `notify`), because two threads reading and writing the same spot at once can overwrite each other's work — a **race condition**.
- A `MessageChannel` gives two workers a direct line to talk without going through the main thread.

The **cluster module** scales *request handling* instead. `node:cluster` starts several copies of your whole program as separate processes; a primary process hands incoming connections to the copies (taking turns, except on Windows), and they all appear to listen on the same port. Each copy is a full Node process with its own memory, so anything kept **in memory** — logged-in **sessions**, caches, counters for **rate limits** — is **not shared**. Move it to a shared store such as Redis (a fast data server) or a **database**.

When you run your app in **containers** — sealed-off packages that each run one app — you'll often skip the cluster module entirely. Run one Node process per container and let the platform (**Kubernetes**, say) start more copies and spread traffic between them with its load balancer.

Each copy is then simpler, a crash affects only one, and each can report its own **health check** (a URL saying "I'm working"). Cluster mode still fits a single server; PM2's cluster mode wraps the same module.

Whatever you choose, make the processes **stateless** — keeping nothing between requests that another copy would need — so any copy can serve any request.
takeaways: Worker pools spread CPU tasks; the cluster module spreads request handling
Transfer or share ArrayBuffers to avoid copying large data; guard shared memory with Atomics
Copies made by the cluster module share nothing — keep state in an outside store
pitfalls: Keeping sessions or rate limits in process memory, then adding cluster and getting inconsistent behaviour.

quiz.q: After switching an app to the cluster module with 8 copies, logged-in users are randomly logged out. Likely cause?
options: The cluster module doesn't support cookies
Sessions were stored in process memory, which each copy has separately
quiz.explain: Each copy is a separate process; an in-memory session store exists only in the copy that created the session.

concepts.name: Running other programs: child_process
concepts.summary: Run other programs with execFile, spawn and fork; stream their output, send them input, and avoid shell injection.
concepts.why: Build tools, command-line tools and servers constantly start other programs: git, ffmpeg, image converters or other Node scripts.
concepts.body:
`node:child_process` starts other programs as **child processes**: separate processes that your program, the parent, starts and controls. Pick the function by what you need.

**`execFile(file, args)`** runs a program and collects all of its output; great for short commands like `git rev-parse HEAD`. Output beyond `maxBuffer` (1 **MB**) is an error.

**`spawn(cmd, args)`** returns a `ChildProcess` whose input, output and error channels (`stdin`, `stdout`, `stderr`) are streams; use it for long-running or chatty programs and large output. `stdio: "inherit"` connects the child straight to your terminal.

**`exec(commandString)`** runs a string through a **shell** — the program behind the terminal that reads what you type, like bash. That makes **pipes** and wildcards (`*.txt`) work, but it is dangerous with **untrusted input**.

**`fork(modulePath)`** starts another Node process with a built-in message channel (**IPC**, inter-process communication), so parent and child exchange objects with `send()` and `on("message")`.

The security rule: **never build a shell command from untrusted input.** `exec(\`convert ${filename} out.png\`)` with a filename like `x; rm -rf ~` runs both commands — a shell **injection attack**. `execFile` and `spawn` without `shell: true` pass each argument straight to the program, so nothing is interpreted by a shell.

The child's **exit code** (0 for success) arrives on the `'close'` event, after its output streams finish, or a `signal` name if it was killed. A non-zero code is not an exception with `spawn` — check it yourself. The promisified `execFile` rejects on a non-zero exit, with `stdout` / `stderr` attached to the error.

Control: `child.kill("SIGTERM")`, the `timeout` and `signal` (AbortSignal) options, and `cwd` and `env` to set the child's folder and environment variables. The `*Sync` variants block the event loop; fine in build scripts, not in servers.

Each child is a full process — tens of milliseconds to start, with its own memory. For heavy JavaScript work prefer worker threads; use child processes for other programs, or to keep risky work fully separate.
takeaways: `execFile` for short commands, `spawn` for streaming, `fork` for Node-to-Node IPC
Never interpolate user input into `exec` or `shell: true` commands
Check the exit code; handle the `'error'` event
pitfalls: Using `exec` with string interpolation of user-controlled values.
Buffering huge output with exec/execFile and hitting maxBuffer.

quiz.q: You need to run ffmpeg on a user-uploaded filename. Which call is safe?
quiz.explain: spawn without a shell passes the filename as a single argument, so shell metacharacters are inert.

concepts.name: Profiling CPU and event-loop performance
concepts.summary: Find bottlenecks with --cpu-prof, DevTools and flame graphs, measure with perf_hooks, and watch event-loop delay.
concepts.why: Performance work without measurement optimises the wrong thing; profiles show where time actually goes.
concepts.body:
Start every performance investigation with a repeatable **load** — a tool like `autocannon` that fires many HTTP requests, or a **benchmark** script that times your code — and one number to improve.
