Typical numbers: **latency** (how long each request takes; look at **percentiles** such as p99, the time that 99% of requests beat), **throughput** (requests handled per second) or event-loop delay.

A CPU **profiler** records which functions use processor time:

- `node --cpu-prof app.js` writes a `.cpuprofile` file when the program exits; open it in Chrome DevTools (Performance tab) or VS Code. `--cpu-prof-dir` sets where it goes.
- Or connect DevTools with `--inspect` and record in the Performance panel while the load runs.
- Read it as a **flame graph**: each bar is a function, and wide bars are where time goes. Look for your own functions in wide stacks — JSON conversion, regular expressions, synchronous crypto, deep copies of objects and logging are frequent culprits.
- `node --prof` plus `node --prof-process` is V8's lower-level profiler, handy on servers without a screen or browser.

**Event-loop delay** is the best single health **metric** (measured number) for a Node service: how late callbacks run. `perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay()` gives a **histogram**, a summary of how the delays are spread (`p50`, `p99`, `max`, in nanoseconds). A rising p99 means something synchronous is hogging the thread.

**Measuring code**: `performance.now()` for durations, `performance.mark` / `measure` for named spans, `performance.timerify(fn)` to time a function, and `PerformanceObserver` to collect the results, including garbage-collection events (`entryTypes: ["gc"]`).

Typical fixes, in order of payoff: do less work (cache results, return big lists one page at a time), keep synchronous calls out of code that runs on every request, move heavy calculations to worker threads, and only then fine-tune individual lines. Time small changes carefully: V8 keeps re-optimising code while it runs, so naive timing loops mislead. Profile again after each change.
takeaways: Measure under realistic load before optimising
`--cpu-prof` and flame graphs show where CPU time goes
Event-loop delay (p99) is the key health metric
Cut wasted work and synchronous calls before fine-tuning
pitfalls: Optimising based on intuition or a micro-benchmark without profiling the real workload.

quiz.q: Your API's p99 latency spikes while CPU is moderate and the DB is fast. Which metric best confirms the event loop is being blocked?
quiz.explain: High event-loop delay means callbacks are running late because synchronous work occupies the thread.

concepts.name: Security essentials for Node apps
concepts.summary: Harden Node services: package hygiene, injection, path traversal, secrets, and the permission model.
concepts.why: Node apps run with your full powers and pull in hundreds of packages; small mistakes become breaches.
concepts.body:
Most Node security holes come from a handful of mistakes.

**Supply chain.** Every package you install — and every package those packages install — is code you run. Keep the lock file, install with `npm ci`, run `npm audit` on every automated build (**CI**), keep dependencies current and beware of names that imitate popular packages with a typo. `npm ci --ignore-scripts` blocks scripts that packages run during install.

**Injection.** Never paste untrusted input into text that something else will interpret: database queries in **SQL** (use **parameterised queries**, which send the values separately from the query), shell commands (`execFile` with an args array, not `exec`), or `eval` / `new Function`.

The same goes for **regular expressions** built from user input, or badly written ones run on it: some take exponentially long on crafted text (**ReDoS**) and freeze the event loop.

**Path traversal.** A user-supplied file name like `../../etc/passwd` climbs out of your folder. Resolve the full path and check it is still inside the allowed folder before reading.

**Prototype pollution.** Every object inherits from one shared prototype object, reachable as `__proto__`. Merging untrusted JSON into an object, level by level, can set properties on it and change every object's behaviour. Check input against a **schema** (a description of the allowed shape), use `Object.create(null)` or `Map` for lookup tables, and avoid hand-written deep merges.

**Denial of service** — making your service unusable. Limit request body sizes, set timeouts, return large lists one page at a time (**pagination**), and keep heavy calculations off the main thread.

**Secrets.** Load passwords and keys from environment variables or a **secrets manager** (a service that stores them securely); never log them or save them with your code. Compare secret **access tokens** (keys that callers send to prove who they are) with `crypto.timingSafeEqual`, which takes the same time whether or not they match, so attackers can't guess them one character at a time.

**Least privilege** — give code only the access it needs. Don't run as the all-powerful root user. Node 22 includes a **permission model**: start with `--permission` and the process cannot touch the file system, start child processes or start worker threads unless you allow it, e.g. `--allow-fs-read=/app --allow-fs-write=/tmp`.

It limits the damage compromised code can do, but it is not a **sandbox** that can safely contain deliberately malicious code. Keep Node itself patched: security releases come out for LTS versions regularly.
takeaways: Lock file + `npm ci` + `npm audit`; keep dependencies few
Use parameterised queries and avoid shells to prevent injection
Resolve and check paths to stop path traversal
`--permission` restricts files, child processes and workers
pitfalls: Checking `userPath.includes('..')` instead of resolving and comparing the final path.
Treating the permission model as a sandbox for untrusted code.

quiz.q: A route serves files with readFile(path.join(root, req.query.name)). What's the main risk?
options: Path traversal to files outside root
quiz.explain: A name with ../ segments can resolve outside the root directory unless you resolve and check it.

quiz.q: What does starting Node with --permission do by default?
options: Denies file system access, child processes and workers unless explicitly allowed
Encrypts all files the process writes
Runs the process as an unprivileged OS user
quiz.explain: The permission model restricts fs, child_process and worker_threads until you grant access with --allow-* flags.

concepts.name: V8 memory, leaks and heap snapshots
concepts.summary: Learn how V8 organises memory and garbage collection, size it for containers, and find memory leaks with heap snapshots.
concepts.why: Memory leaks are the classic slow-burning incident in long-running live services.
concepts.body:
V8 keeps your objects in the **heap**, the large area of memory managed by the garbage collector; each isolate (each worker thread) has its own. It is generational:

- **New space** (the young generation) holds fresh objects. A fast *scavenger* copies the survivors elsewhere; most objects die here cheaply.
- **Old space** holds objects that survived a couple of scavenges. It is cleaned by **mark-sweep-compact** — mark what is still reachable, sweep away the rest, then pack the survivors together — mostly in the background, with some short pauses.
- Large-object space, code space and a few others hold special cases.

`Buffer`s and `ArrayBuffer`s live *outside* the JavaScript heap (counted in `process.memoryUsage().external` and `arrayBuffers`), so the process's total memory, its **RSS** (resident set size), can exceed the heap size.

The old-space limit is set by `--max-old-space-size` (in MB). The default depends on the Node version and the memory it detects, so set it explicitly when running in **containers**, which have a fixed memory limit. Leave room for memory outside the heap: a common choice is about 75% of the container limit. When the heap can't grow, V8 crashes with "JavaScript heap out of memory".

A **leak** in JavaScript means something still *references* data you no longer need. The usual suspects: caches and Maps that only ever grow, listeners added per request, closures kept alive by timers, global arrays used as queues, and per-request data stored on long-lived objects.

To find one, compare **heap snapshots**:

- Take a snapshot, run load, take another (DevTools Memory tab via `--inspect`, `v8.writeHeapSnapshot()`, or `--heapsnapshot-signal=SIGUSR2`).
- Use the Comparison view to see which kinds of object grew, then follow their **retainers** — the objects holding references to them — back to whatever keeps them alive.
- Snapshots pause the process and need roughly twice the heap in memory; avoid them on a struggling live instance that has no memory to spare.

Cheaper signals: `--trace-gc`, `v8.getHeapStatistics()`, and `--heapsnapshot-near-heap-limit=N` to capture evidence automatically before an out-of-memory crash. Use `WeakMap`, `WeakRef` and caches with a size limit (such as LRU caches, which drop the least recently used entries) to make what you keep explicit.
takeaways: Young generation is scavenged cheaply; old space uses mark-sweep-compact
Set `--max-old-space-size` below the container limit, leaving headroom
Leaks are unwanted references; compare heap snapshots and follow retainers
Buffers live outside the JS heap
pitfalls: Raising `--max-old-space-size` to hide a leak, which only delays the crash.
Taking heap snapshots on an instance with no spare memory and triggering the OOM yourself.

quiz.q: Heap usage climbs steadily under constant load and never drops after GC. What's the next diagnostic step?
options: Take two heap snapshots under load and compare them
quiz.explain: Comparing snapshots shows which objects accumulate and what retains them; raising the limit just postpones the crash.

concepts.name: Native addons and Node-API
concepts.summary: How C/C++ and Rust code plugs into Node through Node-API, how addons are built and shipped, and when to avoid them.
concepts.why: Many popular packages (database connectors, image processing, password hashing) are native addons; you need to debug, ship and occasionally write them.
concepts.body:
A **native addon** is a ready-built library file (ending in `.node`) that Node loads like a module. It lets JavaScript call C, C++ or Rust code: to reuse an existing library (libvips for images, SQLite), to reach operating-system features Node doesn't expose, or occasionally for raw speed.

Modern addons use **Node-API** (N-API), a stable C interface maintained by Node itself. Its key property is a stable **ABI** (the low-level rules by which ready-built files call each other): an addon **compiled** against Node-API version N runs on every later Node version without rebuilding. Older addons used V8's internals directly (often through a helper called NAN) and had to be rebuilt for every major Node version. Wrappers make Node-API pleasant: `node-addon-api` for C++, `napi-rs` for Rust.

Building and shipping:

- `node-gyp` (with a `binding.gyp` file) or `cmake-js` compile the addon; this needs Python and a C/C++ **compiler** on the machine.
- Because users rarely have compilers, packages ship **prebuilt binaries** — files already compiled for each operating system and processor type — via `prebuildify`, or as separate optional packages per platform (the approach napi-rs uses).
- In an ES module, load a `.node` file with `createRequire(import.meta.url)` and `require()`.

Writing one, the rules that bite:

- JavaScript values are only valid within a **handle scope** (a short-lived region the C++ code works in); keep long-lived ones as **references**.
- Never block the main thread: long work belongs in an `AsyncWorker`, which runs on libuv's thread pool.

Two more rules concern threads:

- Calling back into JavaScript from other threads requires a **thread-safe** function.
- An addon can be loaded by several worker threads at once, so keep its state per instance (`napi_set_instance_data`), not in C++ **global variables**.

Before reaching for an addon, consider **WebAssembly** (WASM): a portable format for ready-built code that Node runs safely in a **sandbox**, with no compile step for users and often enough speed. Many former native packages now ship WebAssembly builds.
takeaways: Node-API gives a stable ABI: build once, run on later Node versions
Ship prebuilt binaries; users shouldn't need compilers
Do long work in AsyncWorker; use thread-safe functions for cross-thread callbacks
Consider WebAssembly before writing an addon
pitfalls: Doing heavy work synchronously inside an addon function, blocking the event loop.

quiz.q: Why did the move from NAN to Node-API matter so much for addon users?
options: Node-API addons run in a separate process
Node-API automatically converts C++ to JavaScript
Node-API is ABI-stable, so addons needn't be recompiled for each Node major
Node-API removes the need for a C compiler entirely
quiz.explain: ABI stability means one compiled binary keeps working across Node versions.

concepts.name: AsyncLocalStorage and async context
concepts.summary: Carry request-scoped context such as request IDs through async calls with AsyncLocalStorage, and know what async_hooks underlies it.
concepts.why: Logging, tracing and per-request data without passing a context argument through every function.
concepts.body:
In a server, many requests take turns on one thread, so a global "current request" variable is wrong as soon as you `await`. **`AsyncLocalStorage`** (from `node:async_hooks`) solves this: it gives each logical chain of async work its own store, which follows the code through `await`, promise callbacks, timers and event-emitter callbacks created inside that chain.

The class is small:

- `als.run(store, fn)` — run `fn` with `store` as the context; everything `fn` starts asynchronously sees the same store.
- `als.getStore()` — read the current store anywhere below, or `undefined` outside any `run`.
- `als.enterWith(store)` — set the store for the rest of the current synchronous code; avoid it except in special integrations.

The classic use is a **request ID**: **middleware** (code that runs for every request before your handler) calls `als.run({ requestId }, next)`, and your logger reads `als.getStore()?.requestId`. Every log line from one request then carries the same ID without passing anything around. Tracing tools such as OpenTelemetry and APM agents use the same mechanism.

Problems come from context captured at the wrong moment. Packages that keep their own list of callbacks to run later (some database **connection pools** do) may run your callback in another request's context. `AsyncResource.bind(fn)` or `AsyncLocalStorage.bind(fn)` captures the current context into a function, so it runs with the right store later. Also keep stores small and never cache them globally — they hold references for as long as the async chain lives.

Under the hood, Node 22 builds this on **async_hooks** (`createHook` with `init` / `before` / `after` callbacks for every async resource), plus promise hooks. That low-level part is costly, and its hook-based functions are discouraged for application code; use `AsyncLocalStorage` instead. Node 22 also offers `--experimental-async-context-frame` (the default from Node 24), which keeps the context in a slot V8 carries along with each continuation, making propagation much cheaper.
takeaways: `als.run(store, fn)` scopes a store to everything `fn` starts asynchronously
`getStore()` reads it anywhere below — ideal for request IDs and tracing
Use `bind` when a library runs your callback from a shared queue
Prefer AsyncLocalStorage over raw async_hooks
pitfalls: Storing the current request in a module-level variable, which leaks between concurrent requests.

quiz.q: Two requests interleave across awaits. Why does AsyncLocalStorage return the right requestId for each?
options: The store is attached to each async flow and propagates through awaits and callbacks it creates
It locks the event loop per request
It stores data in thread-local storage on separate threads
It reads the ID from the socket each time
quiz.explain: Context follows the async continuation chain created inside run(), not the global execution order.

concepts.name: diagnostics_channel and tracing
concepts.summary: Publish and subscribe to named diagnostic events with diagnostics_channel and TracingChannel, the hooks APM tools use.
concepts.why: It is how modern Node and packages let monitoring tools see inside them (observability) without patching their code.
concepts.body:
Monitoring and tracing tools used to **monkey-patch** library internals — replace a library's functions from the outside while the program runs — to measure them. That is fragile and breaks whenever the library changes. **`node:diagnostics_channel`** replaces it with an explicit **publish/subscribe** (pub/sub) system: libraries announce events on named channels, tools listen.

- A library creates a named channel, `dc.channel("mylib:query")`, and calls `channel.publish(message)` at interesting points.
- A monitoring tool runs `dc.subscribe("mylib:query", handler)` to receive those messages.
- `channel.hasSubscribers` is false when nobody listens, so the library can skip building messages entirely; publishing with no subscribers costs almost nothing.

Name channels with a module prefix (`undici:request:create`, `mylib:query`) to avoid clashes. Subscribers run **synchronously** inside `publish`, so they must be fast and must not throw — exceptions are reported as uncaught but don't break the publisher.

For operations with a start and an end, **`TracingChannel`** standardises five channels — `start`, `end`, `asyncStart`, `asyncEnd`, `error` — and helpers that wrap a function: `tracingChannel.tracePromise(fn, context)` publishes them around a promise-returning call. The same `context` object flows through all events, so a subscriber can store a start time in `start` and compute the duration in `asyncEnd`.

Node itself already publishes: `http.client.request.start`, `http.server.request.start`, `net` connection events, worker thread creation, and **undici** (the engine behind `fetch`) publishes the life cycle of each request. OpenTelemetry instrumentations increasingly subscribe here.

Combine it with **AsyncLocalStorage**: `channel.bindStore(als, transform)` sets a store when the channel's events run, so a trace becomes the active context for the code inside.

If you write a library, adding a few channels is a cheap, high-value way to make it observable.
takeaways: Libraries publish to named channels; tools subscribe — no monkey-patching
Publishing without subscribers is nearly free; check `hasSubscribers` before building messages
TracingChannel standardises start/end/asyncStart/asyncEnd/error with a shared context
Node core and undici already publish channels
pitfalls: Doing slow work or throwing inside a subscriber, which runs synchronously in the publisher's path.

quiz.q: What problem does diagnostics_channel primarily solve?
options: Letting tools observe library internals through explicit events instead of monkey-patching
quiz.explain: It is a low-overhead pub/sub designed specifically for diagnostics and instrumentation.

concepts.name: Graceful shutdown and production lifecycle
concepts.summary: Shut down without dropping requests: handle stop signals, let open connections finish, close resources in order, and report readiness.
concepts.why: Every deploy (shipping a new version) and every automatic scale-down stops processes; done badly, users see errors every time.
concepts.body:
Platforms that run containers — **orchestrators** such as Kubernetes — stop a process by sending **SIGTERM**, the polite "please stop" signal. They wait a grace period (30 s by default in Kubernetes), then send **SIGKILL**, which ends the process instantly. A **graceful shutdown** uses that window to finish work in progress.

**1. Stop receiving traffic.** Make your **readiness check** — a **health check** URL the load balancer uses to ask "can you take requests?" — start failing, so it stops sending you new ones. In Kubernetes that change takes a moment to spread, so wait briefly before closing the listener.

**2. Stop accepting connections** with `server.close(callback)`. It stops listening and (since Node 19) also closes idle **keep-alive** connections, ones held open waiting for a next request. But the callback fires only when *every* connection has ended: requests in progress, slow uploads, **server-sent events** streams and **WebSockets** (connections that stay open for live updates) all keep it waiting.

**3. Drain connections.** Let in-flight requests finish and tell long-lived streams to wind down. After a deadline, `server.closeAllConnections()` forcibly closes whatever is left.

**4. Finish background work** — queues, timers, pending writes — and close resources in reverse order of creation: HTTP server, then job consumers, then database connection pools, then flush logs.

**5. Exit**, with a timer as a safety net: `setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 10_000).unref()`. `unref()` means the timer itself doesn't keep the process alive.

Watch out for your app being **PID 1**, the first process in a container. Linux gives it no default signal behaviour, so without a handler Node ignores SIGTERM there — and `npm start` as the container's start command may not pass signals on at all. Run `node` directly (`CMD ["node", "server.js"]`) or put a tiny init program such as `tini` in front.

Track what keeps the process alive with `ref` / `unref`: anything still referenced (intervals, open connections) prevents a natural exit; `process.getActiveResourcesInfo()` lists them when shutdown hangs.

Make shutdown **idempotent** — safe to run twice — because SIGTERM and SIGINT may both arrive, and test it by sending signals while the service is under load.
takeaways: SIGTERM → fail readiness → close server → drain connections → close resources → exit
`server.close` waits for open connections; force stragglers with `closeAllConnections`
Use an unref'd timer as a forced-exit safety net
Run node directly (or under tini) so it receives signals in containers
pitfalls: Using `npm start` as the container command so SIGTERM never reaches Node.
Calling `process.exit()` immediately on SIGTERM and cutting off in-flight requests.

quiz.q: During shutdown, server.close()'s callback hasn't fired after 30 seconds. Most likely reason?
options: The operating system is still holding the port
A long-lived connection such as a server-sent events stream or WebSocket is still open
close() requires a SIGKILL to complete
The event loop is stuck in the check phase
quiz.explain: close() waits for every open connection to end; long-lived streams must be ended or force-closed with closeAllConnections().

quiz.q: Why call .unref() on the forced-exit timer?
options: So it doesn't by itself keep the process alive if shutdown finishes
To make it run on another thread
quiz.explain: An unref'd timer still fires if the process is alive, but won't prevent a natural exit.
